analysis.one_liner: Caps seniors' combined Medicare drug out-of-pocket costs at $2,600 a year.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors in September 2018, never got a committee vote and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare splits prescription drug coverage between two programs — Part D for drugs you pick up at a pharmacy and Part B for drugs given in a doctor's office — and each has its own cost-sharing rules, so a senior can face unlimited combined drug bills in a year. This bill would set a single combined limit: once a person's out-of-pocket drug costs hit $2,600 in a year (in 2021), they would owe nothing more for their drugs for the rest of the year. The federal government would reimburse the insurance plans for the cost-sharing they give up, so the plans are paid back in full.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who face high prescription drug bills — especially those taking expensive specialty drugs — would stop owing cost-sharing once their annual out-of-pocket drug spending reached the cap.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries with high drug costs

how_it_helps.text: Starting in 2021, once a Part D enrollee's yearly out-of-pocket drug costs reach $2,600, all beneficiary coinsurance for covered Part D drugs for the rest of the year is eliminated [S3].

The cap is a true combined limit: costs paid for Part B drugs (like drugs infused in a doctor's office) count toward it, and once it is reached Medicare pays 100% of the cost of Part B drugs for the rest of the year instead of the usual 80% [S3].
The cap rises each year with average per-capita drug spending under Part D, so it stays in place over time [S3].

The bill counts certain state and federal assistance programs (such as State Pharmaceutical Assistance Programs and the AIDS Drug Assistance Program) toward reaching the cap, so people getting help from those programs are not penalized [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through the Medicare program, which would pay drug plans a subsidy covering all the cost-sharing the plans no longer collect from beneficiaries — spending that grows automatically as drug prices rise, since the bill includes no drug price controls.

drawbacks.text: The bill pays drug prices as charged: the government reimburses plans for every dollar of cost-sharing it eliminates, with no mechanism to lower drug prices themselves, so federal spending rises as prices rise [S3].
The cap applies only to people enrolled in stand-alone prescription drug plans, not to the many beneficiaries who get their drug coverage through Medicare Advantage plans [S3].

Out-of-pocket costs count toward the cap only if paid by the individual or family without reimbursement from other insurance or third parties, which can leave out people who rely on outside help not on the approved list [S3].
A fair-minded objection: covering cost-sharing without restraining prices can push more drug spending onto the federal budget, which in the long run competes with other public priorities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors with serious drug needs, the benefit is real and immediate: a hard ceiling on what they can be billed for prescriptions each year. The honest cost is that the bill funds that ceiling by paying current drug prices, so it shifts costs to taxpayers rather than lowering them, and it leaves out Medicare Advantage enrollees. A stronger bill would have paired the cap with price controls or negotiation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors, sent to two House committees, referred to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom O'Halleran introduced the bill on September 28, 2018, less than three months before the 115th Congress ended [S1].
It was referred to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced [S5].
On October 12, 2018, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was ever taken on it [S5].
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers avoided a new open-ended federal subsidy that would have paid drug prices as charged. Seniors with high drug costs gained nothing: they still have no combined out-of-pocket limit covering both Medicare drug programs from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers; seniors with high drug costs gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Tom O'Halleran
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and took no further action before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No committee or floor votes were ever taken, and no Republican or Democratic cosponsor joined, so the partisan shape of support and opposition was never tested.

industries.note: Once a senior hits the cap, the federal government picks up the full cost of their drugs at whatever prices manufacturers charge, with no price negotiation anywhere in the bill. Seniors get relief from the cap, but the industry's gain comes at taxpayers' expense, and its pricing power is untouched.

industries.industry: Part D prescription drug plan sponsors
industries.note: Plans would lose cost-sharing revenue from high-cost enrollees but be fully reimbursed by a new federal subsidy, so they give up nothing. Their role as the channel through which the new protection flows is locked in.
